blocks.text: This is the view of the Latin Fathers. Which is surprising, since in the Vulgate version one reads at Nahum III, 16. The bruchus spread out and flew away, and in the Greek, Βροῦχος ὥρμησε, καὶ ἐξεπετάσθη [Brouchos hōrmēse, kai exepetasthē]. And at Levit. XI, 22. the bruchus is counted among the winged [col. 448] locusts. Accordingly the Greek Fathers attribute flight and wings to the bruchus. Thus Cyril says of it on Nahum ch. 3: Φασὶ γὰρ, ὅτι, πιπτούσης χαλάζης, καὶ ὑετῶν καταρηγγνυμένων ἀδρανὴς εἰς πτῆσιν ὁ βροῦχος, καταδεδευμένων αὐτῷ τῶν πτερῶν [Phasi gar, hoti, piptousēs chalazēs, kai hyetōn katarēngnymenōn adranēs eis ptēsin ho brouchos, katadedeumenōn autō tōn pterōn]; For they say that when hail falls and rains burst forth, the bruchus becomes weak for flight, its wings being soaked. And Theodoret in the same place, of the same: Τῆς ἡλιακῆς προσβαλλούσης ἀκτῖνος ἀνίσταται, καὶ πετάννυσι τὰ πτερὰ, καὶ εἰς ἕτερον μεταβαίνει τόπον [Tēs hēliakēs proballousēs aktinos anistatai, kai petannysi ta ptera, kai eis heteron metabainei topon]; When the ray of the sun strikes it, it rises, spreads its wings, and moves elsewhere. Indeed the same author, on Amos VII, 1., openly distinguishes the bruchus from the young of locusts: Ἐπιγονὴν δὲ ἀκρίδων, he says, ἐκάλησε τὸν Ἀσσύριον, βροῦχον δὲ τὸν Βαβυλώνιον [Epigonēn de akridōn … ekalēse ton Assyrion, brouchon de ton Babylōnion]; He called the Assyrian the young of locusts, but the Babylonian the bruchus. The Greek translators too, at Levit. XI, 22., seem to have distinguished the bruchus from the common locust not only by age but also by species. But the use of the word varied. For among the Ionians βροῦκος [broukos] was a species of locust, and among the Cypriots βροῦκας [broukas] was the green locust, but among the Tarentines the attelabus. Hesychius: Βροῦκος· ἀκρίδων εἶδος, Ἴωνες. Κύπριοι δὲ τὴν χλωρὰν ἀκρίδα βροῦκαν· Ταραντῖνοι δὲ ἀττέλεβον [Broukos; akridōn eidos, Iōnes. Kyprioi de tēn chlōran akrida broukan; Tarantinoi de attelebon], that is, ἀττέλαβον [attelabon]. Thus for Theophrastus, in the little book On the animals that appear suddenly, the βροῦκος [broukos] is a species of attelabus: Χαλεπαὶ μὲν οὖν, he says, αἱ ἀκρίδες, χαλεπώτεροι δὲ οἱ ἀττέλαβοι, καὶ τούτων μάλιστα οὓς καλοῦσι βρούκους [Chalepai men oun … hai akrides, chalepōteroi de hoi attelaboi, kai toutōn malista hous kalousi broukous]; Locusts indeed are harmful, but attelabi are more harmful, and most of all those they call bruci. So one must read, instead of the corrupt βαρούκτους [baroukt ous].

Thus for the older writers the attelabus cannot be the immature young of the locust, since they more than once mention the brood and eggs of the attelabus: Aristotle, History book 5, ch. 29: Ὁμοίως δὲ τίκτουσι καὶ οἱ ἀττέλαβοι [Homoiōs de tiktousi kai hoi attelaboi], The attelabi too give birth in the same way. And a little later: Φθείρεται δὲ αὐτῶν τὰ ὠὰ ὑπὸ τῶν μετοπωρινῶν ὑδάτων [Phtheiretai de autōn ta ōa hypo tōn metopōrinōn hydatōn]; Their eggs are destroyed by the autumn rains. Plutarch in Isis: Λήμνιοι [III, 263] κορύδους ἐτίμησαν τὰ τῶν ἀττελάβων εὑρίσκοντας ὠὰ, καὶ κόπτοντας [Lēmnioi korydous etimēsan ta tōn attelabōn heuriskontas ōa, kai koptontas]; the Lemnians honoured larks, because they found the eggs of the attelabi and broke them. The same author seems everywhere to take ἀττέλαβον [attelabon] or ἀττέλεβον [attelebon] for the locust in general: as in the Symposiaca book 2, ch. 3, where he says that the egg generates δίποδα τὸν ὄρνιν, καὶ ἄποδα τὸν ὄφιν, καὶ πολύποδα τὸν ἀττέλεβον [dipoda ton ornin, kai apoda ton ophin, kai polypoda ton attelebon], the two-footed bird, the footless serpent, and the many-footed attelabus. And a little below, when in the servile war in Sicily much blood had been shed and corpses lay rotting unburied on the ground, πλῆθος, he says, ἀττελέβων ἐξήνθησε, καὶ τὸν σῖτον ἔφθειρον, πανταχοῦ σχεδασθέντες ἐπὶ τὴν νῆσον [plēthos … attelebōn exēnthēse, kai ton siton ephtheiron, pantachou schedasthentes epi tēn nēson], a multitude of attelabi sprang up, which, scattered everywhere over the island, ruined the crops. Of the same kind is the fact that in Eubulus' riddle in Athenaeus book 10 the ichneumon is called ἀττελεβόφθαλμος [attelebophthalmos] instead of ἀκριδοφθάλμῳ [akridophthalmō]. Yet this is certain: the attelabus was small within the locust kind, and ἄπτερον [apteron, wingless]. Hesychius: ἀττέλεβος· ἀκρὶς μικρά [attelebos; akris mikra]. Pliny book 29, ch. 5: The smallest of the locusts, without wings, which they call attelabi. Hence the Greek translators at Nahum III, 17: Ἐξήλατο ὡς ἀττέλαβος [Exēlato hōs attelabos], It leapt like an attelabus, attributing to it not flight but leaping. Indeed it seems to be named from leaping. It is well known that φ and β are often interchanged. Thus among the Macedonians Φίλιππος [Philippos] was Βίλιππος [Bilippos]; Φερονίκη [Pheronikē], Βερονίκη [Beronikē]; Φρύγες [Phryges], Βρίγες [Briges]. φάλαινα [phalaina] and balaena [whale] sound the same; so do ἀμφιλαφὴς [amphilaphēs] and ἀμφιλαβής [amphilabēs]. Πιστάκιον [Pistakion] is also written φιστάκιον [phistakion] and βιστάκιον [bistakion]. So I would think that ἀττέλαβον [attelabon] was the same as ἀττέλαφον [attelaphon], that is, leaping deer, or leaping like a deer. For ἄττειν [attein] is to leap, and ἔλαφος [elaphos] is deer, whose agility in leaping is praised at Es. XXXV, 6. To this point is the fact that the Talmudists count among the species of locusts איילא קמצא, as if you said ἀκριδέλαφον [akridelaphon], or deer-locust. The Arabic translator of Nahum, who clings tenaciously to the Greek text, renders the Greek words Ἐξήλατο ὡς ἀττέλαβος [Exēlato hōs attelabos] thus: وثب مثل جرادة سودا [wathaba mithl jarāda sūdā] It leapt like a black locust.
